title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-wip-5
content:
Purpose / context:
This doc captures the current state of our throughput benchmarking harness and the methodology we use to produce repeatable, comparable throughput numbers for the serving runtime. It collects load-gen config conventions, warmup rules, measurement windows, and profiling guidance used by the team.

Status / audience:
- Working doc: intended for engineers running benchmarks, QA, and performance reviews.
- Goal: reduce experiment variability and produce defensible throughput charts (tokens/s, effective FPS, GPU utilization).

High-level goals:
- Measure steady-state throughput while respecting latency SLOs.
- Make runs repeatable across hardware and cluster configs.
- Provide reproducible configs for public benchmarks and internal perf regressions.
- Surface common bottlenecks (CPU scheduling, memcpy, kernel launch, batching).

Important definitions (how we use terms here):
- Warmup: period before measurements during which caches, KV caches, kernels, and JITs reach steady state. Not included in reported numbers.
- Steady-state window: contiguous time window used to compute throughput/latency percentiles.
- Effective throughput: tokens generated / second during steady-state window (exclude warmup).
- Concurrency: number of simultaneous requests (not to be confused with batch size).

Metrics we capture (always report units):
- tokens_per_sec (tokens/s) - primary throughput metric.
- requests_per_sec (req/s) - helpful for routing-style workloads.
- latency_p50/p95/p99 (ms) - end-to-end at the request granularity.
- gpu_utilization (percent) - average GPU util during window (nvidia-smi sample).
- mem_bandwidth_util (GB/s) - if available from profiling.
- kernel_occupancy - from profilers (nsight / nvprof).
- cpu_user/cpu_sys (percent) - host CPU usage aggregated.
- batching_efficiency - produced tokens / theoretical max given batch config.

Harness components (what we run):
1) Load generator (loadgen): config-driven program that issues requests with realistic prompt and seq-len distribution. Supports: fixed-seq, distribution-based seqlens, streaming vs non-streaming, and tool-calling stubs.
2) Driver/orchestrator: spins up the serving processes (local or k8s), configures model variants, collects logs and metrics, and starts loadgen.
3) Collector: aggregates metrics (prometheus, nvidia-smi, torchmetrics) and stores raw traces.
4) Profiler hooks: optional, attach torch.profiler / nsight during specific windows to capture kernel-level data.

Repeatability practices (must do):
- Use pinned CPU isolation: taskset/cgroups to pin loadgen and server threads to specific cores.
- Fix random seeds for token sampling where applicable.
- Run on a known image/build and include full git commit / docker image tag in metadata.
- Disable background jittering services (e.g., cron, package managers) on benchmark hosts.
- Use performance governor (no power save) and identical BIOS settings across nodes.
- Reboot between major config changes.
- For k8s runs: use static node pools, disable autoscaler, and reserve nodes for benchmark jobs.

Warmup rules (recommended):
- Short model loads (<=1B parameters): minimum warmup = 30s + 10s per active worker.
- Medium models (1B-10B): 60s + 20s per worker.
- Large models (>10B): 120s + 30s per worker and explicit KV cache priming.
- KV cache priming: run a set of requests that exercise typical prefix lengths (samples from the same distribution) until per-token kernel times stabilize (<5% variance over 3 consecutive samples).
- Dynamic batching warmup: increase QPS gradually over the first 50-100s to let batching queues converge.
- Report: warmup duration chosen and a short warmup convergence plot (tokens/sec vs time).

Measurement windows and aggregation: 
- After warmup, record metrics for N minutes (default N=5). For graphs spanning concurrency sweep, keep window constant.
- Sliding-window sanity check: compute throughput over 30s windows to verify no large outliers. If variance >10% across windows, rerun.
- Report median across 3 independent runs (same config) and include min/max.
- Always attach raw time-series for audit.

Load generator config conventions (example YAML snippet used by loadgen):

loadgen:
  model: "redwood/redwood-7b-v1"
  seq_distribution: "mix-small-large"  # see distributions/ directory for presets
  concurrency: 32
  request_rate_limit: null     # null => unthrottled, else QPS cap
  batch_size_hint: 8           # soft hint for batching in the runtime
  streaming: false
  prompt_shard: "prod-sample-2024-09"
  seed: 42
  duration_s: 420             # total run duration, includes warmup
  warmup_s: 120
  warmup_kv_priming: true

Notes on seq_distribution:
- Presets: fixed-128, fixed-256, fixed-1024, mix-small-large (60% short 64 tokens, 30% 256, 10% 1024), chat-dialogue (turns of 32-512).
- Use the same distribution when comparing model variants.

Profiling guidance (when to turn on heavy profilers):
- Run high-overhead profilers (nsight / torch.profiler with shapes/stack) only on a short slice after stable warmup (e.g., 30s), not during whole measurement window.
- Collect per-request tracing (lightweight) for latency distribution and batching patterns.
- Capture nvtx ranges around batching and token-generation loops.
- Save profiler outputs with git/dockertag+timestamp in the filename.

Common bottlenecks and heuristics to spot them:
- GPU-bound: tokens/s scales with number of GPUs or model size; gpu_utilization high (>80%), CPU low.
- CPU pre/post-processing bound: CPU at 80-100% while GPU low - check memcpy, tokenization, RPC overhead.
- PCIe bandwidth/memcpy bound: if memcopy times dominate kernel time and mem_bandwidth_util near max.
- Kernel launch overhead / small-kernel fragmentation: many tiny kernels and low occupancy - consider kernel fusion or larger micro-batches.
- KV cache thrashing: if latency increases over time or throughput drops with longer prefixes.
- Lock contention: profiling shows significant time in pthread_mutex/lock - look at batching queues and global locks.

Experiment matrix (recommended sweep):
- Vary concurrency: [1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128] or until saturation observed.
- Vary batch_size_hint: [1,2,4,8,16,32] to find sweet spot.
- Vary seq_distribution presets.
- Repeat for quantization/precision modes (fp16, int8 where available).
- For each point: run 3 trials, median as canonical.

Reporting conventions (what to include in a perf PR):
- Full config file used (attach in PR).
- Image / commit id + docker tag.
- Hardware spec: GPU model, driver, CUDA, CPU model, node type, BIOS settings.
- Raw CSV time-series for tokens/s, latency percentiles, gpu_utilization.
- Profiler artifacts (zipped) with short findings summary.
- Plots: throughput vs concurrency, latency p50/p95 vs concurrency, gpu_utilization vs concurrency.

Checklist before merging numbers to master results: 
- [ ] Warmup config documented and justified.
- [ ] 3 independent runs completed and median reported.
- [ ] Raw logs and metrics attached.
- [ ] Profiling artifacts for at least one config attached.
- [ ] All environment variables and build tags recorded.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Determine minimal stable warmup heuristic based on model size & KV cache characteristics (automation ticket: jira SERV-2201).
- Add a library to synthesize realistic chat-turn sequences derived from anonymized prod traces (privacy-preserving).
- Improve loadgen to support closed-loop workloads (variable server-side state per request).

Quick run example (local dev):
- start server: ./run_local_server --model redwood-7b --port 8080 --gpu 0
- run loadgen: python tools/loadgen.py --config examples/mix-small-large.yaml --target http://localhost:8080/generate
- collect metrics: prometheus scrapes + nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --loop-ms=1000

Notes / heuristics from recent runs:
- For redwood-7b, batch_size_hint 8 and concurrency 32 gave best tokens/s in the TF32 kernels on A100; increasing to 64 raised tail latency significantly.
- Small-sequence-heavy distributions often expose kernel-launch overhead; increasing micro-batch reduces overhead but hurt latency for single request workloads.

References:
- Internal: confluence:SERVING-Throughput-Harness (live doc); jira:SERV-987 for perf regression template.
- External references: nsight and torch.profiler docs for kernel tracing.

Appendix: example minimal config used for perf PR (single file):
{
  "meta": {
    "run_id": "bench-redwood-7b-2024-11-01",
    "git_commit": "abc1234"
  },
  "loadgen": {
    "model": "redwood-7b",
    "seq_distribution": "fixed-256",
    "concurrency": 32,
    "batch_size_hint": 8,
    "warmup_s": 120,
    "duration_s": 420
  },
  "environment": {
    "gpu": "A100-40GB",
    "cuda": "12.1"
  }
}

If you run these and get surprising variance, ping me (Jamie) and attach the raw time series and docker tag.

-- end --
